title: On Anti-Corruption and Clean Governance
source: From Third World to First / Speeches at Parliament
content: Corruption is a disease that eats away at the fabric of society. From the day we took office in 1959, we decided that if we wanted to build a nation, Singapore had to be spotless. If the top leadership is corrupt, the entire civil service falls apart. We paid ministers and civil servants competitive market salaries to attract top talent and remove any financial pressure or temptation to accept bribes. But high pay alone is not enough; punishment for corruption must be swift, severe, and apply to everyone without exception, regardless of position or political standing. Clean government is not an accident; it is a relentless administrative choice maintained every single day.

title: On Small Nations, Sovereignty, and Geopolitics
source: Speech at the S. Rajaratnam Lecture & Memoirs
content: A small nation like Singapore must take the world as it is, not as we wish it to be. We live in a turbulent region surrounded by larger neighbors. Therefore, a small state must be exceptional. It must be relevant to the rest of the world, offering reliability, strategic value, and economic efficiency that larger nations cannot afford to ignore. We maintain a strong military deterrence through the SAF—a poison shrimp strategy—so that no neighbor thinks attacking us will be easy or free of ruinous cost. Simultaneously, we build balanced alliances with major global powers, including the United States, China, and Europe, maintaining dynamic balance rather than taking rigid sides.

title: On US-China Relations and Global Superpowers
source: One Man's View of the World (2013)
content: The rise of China is a historical reality that the world must accommodate. China is not just another big player; it is the biggest player in the history of the world. The United States must accept that it cannot permanently contain China, while China must understand that asserting regional hegemony aggressively will drive its Asian neighbors into tighter defense relationships with America. Small nations in Asia do not wish to be forced to choose between Washington and Beijing. The ideal future is one of competitive co-existence, where both superpowers engage in economic interdependence while establishing guardrails against military conflict.

title: On Meritocracy, Talent, and Education
content: Singapore's only natural resource is its people. We have no oil, no gold, no vast agricultural land, and not even our own natural water supply at independence. Therefore, meritocracy is our survival strategy. Every Singaporean child must have access to top-tier education regardless of race, language, or social background. Position and promotion in public life must be awarded purely on ability, integrity, and performance, never on family connections or cronyism. However, meritocracy must be tempered with compassion; those who succeed must give back to uplift those who fall behind, ensuring social mobility remains alive across generations.

title: On Racial and Religious Harmony
content: Singapore is not a Chinese nation, a Malay nation, or an Indian nation. It is a multiracial, multicultural, and multilingual nation where every citizen has an equal stake. The traumatic racial riots of the 1960s taught us that racial harmony cannot be left to chance or pious hopes. We enforced strict housing quota policies (Ethnic Integration Policy) in public HDB flats to prevent ethnic enclaves from forming, ensuring children of all races grew up, played, and lived together. We protect freedom of religion while strictly forbidding religious extremism or hate speech from fracturing our social cohesion.

title: On Economic Pragmatism and Water Self-Sufficiency
source: The Singapore Story / National Day Speeches
content: Ideology must serve reality, not the other way around. When we were thrust out of Malaysia in 1965, foreign experts predicted Singapore would collapse. We ignored ideological dogmas of the era—such as import substitution—and instead welcomed foreign multinational corporations (MNCs) to invest, bring technology, and create jobs when others viewed MNCs as neo-colonialists. Look at our water supply: dependent on Johor contracts, we treated water as a national security existential threat. We invested heavily in R&D for desalination and NEWater (recycled water) until we achieved water sovereignty. Always plan for the long term, innovate out of necessity, and execute with relentless discipline.

title: On Hard Work, Discipline, and Personal Resilience
content: Life is a continuous struggle. Nothing worthwhile comes without hard work, discipline, and emotional fortitude. I have spent my whole life standing up, working, planning for Singapore. Even on a sickbed, if I see something going wrong with Singapore, I will get up. Young people must understand that the world does not owe you a living. Success requires continuous learning, adaptability to technological shifts, and a willingness to confront unpleasant truths directly. Be realistic, be pragmatic, keep your integrity intact, and never give up when faced with overwhelming odds.

title: On Rule of Law and Legal System
source: Speech to Singapore Law Society & Cambridge Address
content: Law and order are the foundations of civilized society and economic prosperity. Investors do not bring billions of dollars to a country where laws are arbitrary or judges can be bought. As a lawyer trained at Cambridge, I knew we had to maintain a judicial system of impeccable integrity based on the common law framework. The law must be enforced firmly and impartially. True freedom is not absolute anarchy; true freedom is the security of knowing that your life, family, property, and business are protected under the firm and fair rule of law.
